## Introduction

The Australian Bushfire Weather Risk Explorer is an
interactive data product based on published research
examining the influence of anthropogenic climate change
on extreme bushfire weather risk in Australia.

It focuses on findings related to the 2019/20 Australian
bushfire season.

## Dataset

The package includes the `bushfire_risk` dataset, which
contains nine curated research findings covering:

- Extreme fire weather
- Extreme temperature
- Extreme drought
- The driest month of the fire season
- Natural climate variability

## Loading the dataset

Load the package and inspect the dataset:

```{r}
library(bushfireexplorer)

head(bushfire_risk)
```

You can also inspect its structure:

```{r}
str(bushfire_risk)
```

## Summarising research findings

The `summarise_risk()` function allows users to explore
research findings by indicator and climate scenario.

### View all research findings

```{r}
summarise_risk(data = bushfire_risk)
```

### Filter by risk indicator and climate scenario

For example, users can focus on extreme fire weather
under the present climate:

```{r}
summarise_risk(
  data = bushfire_risk,
  selected_indicator = "Extreme fire weather",
  selected_scenario = "Present climate"
)
```

The function returns matching research records, including
the evidence type, estimate type, numerical estimate,
research finding and limitations.

Qualitative findings are also retained when numerical
estimates are unavailable.

## Launching the Shiny application

Launch the interactive application using:

```{r eval=FALSE}
run_app()
```

Users can select a risk indicator and climate scenario
to explore the corresponding findings.

The application displays numerical estimates where
available, alongside research interpretations and
important limitations.

## Interpreting the findings

The central climate-model estimate indicates that the
probability of a 2019/20-level extreme fire-weather event
under the present climate is approximately 1.8 times
the probability in the early twentieth-century climate.

The conservative lower bound is approximately 1.3 times.

The ERA5 observational estimate is greater than four.
However, observational and model estimates should not
be directly combined because they do not overlap.

Under a climate scenario approximately 2°C warmer,
the estimated probability is approximately eight times
higher, with a conservative lower bound of approximately
four times higher.

These future estimates are based on only two climate
models and involve substantial uncertainty.

## Important limitations

This package presents curated findings from published
research. It does not perform a new climate-model analysis.

Bushfire weather risk does not directly represent actual
fire occurrence or damage. Ignition, vegetation, exposure
and vulnerability also influence bushfire impacts.

Some findings are qualitative and do not have numerical
estimates. These are presented as research descriptions
rather than numerical charts.

## Source

van Oldenborgh et al. (2021). Attribution of the
Australian bushfire risk to anthropogenic climate change.
Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences, 21, 941–960.

https://doi.org/10.5194/nhess-21-941-2021
